metadata.title: Blow up and Blur constructions in algebraic logic

extraction_notes.note: The source has many missing periods and run-on sentences (e.g. 'Such an $\bold M$ exists It is also known...', a sentence ending in 'and' followed by a new paragraph); spans were taken to the nearest real sentence end, so some nodes merge two intended sentences.

Theorems 3.1 and 4.1 marked external: the paper says it gives simpler proofs of Hodkinson's and Andreka-Nemeti's results. Theorem 3.1 has no proof environment; the preceding prose of Section 3 is a sketch linked by uses edges, not a proves edge.

The Ramsey-style argument in 'The relation algebra' (first example) is treated as a prose proof of the claim that follows it; the argument is explicitly incomplete (the needed condition on $k$ is posed as an open problem inside it), so ClP10 is semi_formal.

The neat embedding theorem ${\sf RRA}=\bigcap_k S{\sf Ra}{\sf CA}_{n+k}$ is stated in full but inside the same sentence that applies it; no separate external node is possible without partial overlap, so it stays in the claim's text.

The abstract, introduction and the informal analogy paragraphs of the last subsection (heuristic narrative, no separately stated results) and the restatement 'From a graph Hirsch and Hodkinson constructed...' (a repeat of TP4) were not extracted.

The proof's enumarab items (1),(2) and the {\bf Case} headings were not reported as structure labels by the parser; they were treated as author labels and the nested 'We now show'/'We show that' openers as claim containers.

nodes.name: atom structure (convention)
nodes.statement: In what follows, by an atom structure, we mean an atom structure of any class of completely additive Boolean algebras.
differentia: of any class of completely additive Boolean algebras

nodes.name: Blow up and blur atom structure
nodes.statement: \begin{enumarab} \item A splitting of $N$ is a disjoint union $N\times I$, where $I$ is an infinite set. \item A blur for $N$ is any set $J$. \item An atom structure $\alpha$ is blown up and blurred if, there exists a subset $J'$ of a set $J$ of blurs, possibly empty, such that $\alpha$ has underlying set $X=N\times I \times J'$; the latter atom structure is called a blur of $N$ via $J$, and is denoted by $\alpha(N,J).$ Furthermore, every $j\in J$, induces a non-principal ultrafilter in $\wp(X)$. \item An atom structure $\alpha(N, J)$ reflects $N$, if $N$ is faithfully represented in ${\mathfrak{Cm}}\alpha(N,J)$ \item An atom structure $\alpha(N,J)$ is weak if ${\mathfrak{Tm}}\alpha(N,J)$ is representable. \item An atom structure $\alpha(N, J)$ is very weak ${\mathfrak{Tm}}\alpha(N,J)$ is not representable. \item An atom structure $\alpha(N,J)$ is strong if ${\mathfrak{Cm}}\alpha(N,J)$ is representable. \end{enumarab}
nodes.definiendum: blown up and blurred atom structure $\alpha(N,J)$
nodes.statement_short: Defines splitting $N\times I$, blurs $J$, blown up and blurred atom structures $\alpha(N,J)$, and the notions reflects / weak / very weak / strong.

nodes.name: colour of a label
nodes.statement: The colour of $(\rho, i)$ is defined to be $i$. The \textit{colour} of $(a, i)$ for $a \in {\bf G}$ is $i$.

nodes.name: family $\cal F$ of labelled graphs
nodes.statement: $\cal F$ consists of all complete labelled graphs $\Gamma$ (possibly the empty graph) such that for all distinct $ x, y, z \in \Gamma$, writing $ (a, i) = \Gamma (y, x)$, $ (b, j) = \Gamma (y, z)$, $ (c,l) = \Gamma (x, z)$, we have:\\ \begin{enumarab} \item $| \{ i, j, l \} > 1 $, or \item $ a, b, c \in {\bf G}$ and $ \{ a, b, c \} $ has at least one edge of ${\bf G}$, or \item exactly one of $a, b, c$ -- say, $a$ -- is $\rho$, and $bc$ is an edge of ${\bf G}$, or \item two or more of $a, b, c$ are $\rho$. \end{enumarab}
nodes.statement_short: $\cal F$: complete labelled graphs whose triangles satisfy one of four colour/edge conditions w.r.t. ${\bf G}$.

nodes.name: labelled graph $M$
nodes.statement: One forms a labelled graph $M$ which can be viewed as model of a natural signature, namely, the one with relation symbols $R_{(a, i)}$, for each $a \in {\bf G} \cup \{\rho\}$, $i<n$ and Then one takes a subset $W\subseteq {}^nM$, by roughly dropping assignments that do not satify $(\rho, l)$ for every $l<n$.

nodes.name: set of permitted assignments $W$
nodes.statement: Formally, $W = \{ \bar{a} \in {}^n M : M \models ( \bigwedge_{i < j < n, l < n} \neg (\rho, l)(x_i, x_j))(\bar{a}) \}.$
nodes.statement_short: $W$: $n$-tuples of $M$ no two of whose entries are joined by a $\rho$-labelled edge.

nodes.name: relativized set algebra ${\mathfrak{A}}$
nodes.statement: This algebr, call it ${\mathfrak{A}}$, has universe $\{\phi^M: \phi\in L^n\}$ where $\phi^M=\{s\in W: M\models \phi[s]\}.$

nodes.name: completion ${\mathfrak{C}}$ is not representable
nodes.statement: Its completion is the relativized set algebra ${\mathfrak{C}}$ with universe the larger $\{\phi^M: \phi\in L^n_{\infty,\omega}\}$, which turns out not representable.
conclusions: which turns out not representable

nodes.name: isomorphism ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\sf At}{\mathfrak{A}}\cong{\mathfrak{C}}
nodes.statement: The isomorphism from ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\sf At}{\mathfrak{A}}$ to ${\mathfrak{C}}$ is given by $X\mapsto \bigcup X$.
conclusions: The isomorphism from ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\sf At}{\mathfrak{A}}$ to ${\mathfrak{C}}$ is given by $X\mapsto \bigcup X$

nodes.name: split-and-blur reading of ${\mathfrak{A}}$
nodes.statement: Take the $n$ disjoint copies of $N\times \omega={\bf G}$. Let $a\in {\bf G}\times n$. Then $a\in N\times \omega\times n$. Then for every $(a,i)$ where $a\in N\times \omega$, and $i<n$, we have an atom $R_{a,i}^{{\mathfrak{M}}}\in {\mathfrak{A}}$. The term algebra of ${\mathfrak{A}}$ is generated by those.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: identify the atoms $R_{a,i}$ of ${\mathfrak{A}}$ with $N\times\omega\times n$.

nodes.name: atom structure of ${\mathfrak{A}}$ is weakly represented with $n$ blurs
nodes.statement: Hence ${\mathfrak{N}}\times \omega\times n$ is the atom structure of ${\mathfrak{A}}$ which can be weakly represented using the $n$ blurs, namely the set $\{\rho, i): i<n\}$.
conclusions: ${\mathfrak{N}}\times \omega\times n$ is the atom structure of ${\mathfrak{A}}$ which can be weakly represented using the $n$ blurs

nodes.name: relation algebra atom structure $\alpha({\bf G})$
nodes.statement: We define a relation algebra atom structure $\alpha({\bf G})$ of the form $(\{1'\}\cup ({\bf G}\times n), R_{1'}, \breve{R}, R_;)$. The only identity atom is $1'$. All atoms are self converse, so $\breve{R}=\{(a, a): a \text { an atom }\}.$

nodes.name: colour of an atom of $\alpha({\bf G})$
nodes.statement: The colour of an atom $(a,i)\in {\bf G}\times n$ is $i$. The identity $1'$ has no colour.

nodes.name: consistent triples of $\alpha({\bf G})$
nodes.statement: A triple $(a,b,c)$ of atoms in $\alpha({\bf G})$ is consistent if $R;(a,b,c)$ holds. Then the consistent triples are $(a,b,c)$ where \begin{itemize} \item one of $a,b,c$ is $1'$ and the other two are equal, or \item none of $a,b,c$ is $1'$ and they do not all have the same colour, or \item $a=(a', i), b=(b', i)$ and $c=(c', i)$ for some $i<n$ and $a',b',c'\in {\bf G}$, and there exists at least one graph edge of $G$ in $\{a', b', c'\}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Consistent triples: identity triples, non-monochromatic triples, or monochromatic triples containing a ${\bf G}$-edge.

nodes.name: $\alpha({\bf G})$ is a relation atom structure
nodes.statement: $\alpha({\bf G})$ can be checked to be a relation atom structure.
conclusions: $\alpha({\bf G})$ can be checked to be a relation atom structure

nodes.name: At ${\mathfrak{A}}$ is the basic-matrix atom structure ${\cal M}_n$
nodes.statement: This allows the relation algebra to have an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis and, in fact, the atom structure of ${\mathfrak{A}}$ is isomorphic (as a cylindric algebra atom structure) to the atom structure ${\cal M}_n$ of all $n$-dimensional basic matrices over the relation algebra atom structure $\alpha({\bf G})$.
conclusions:
the atom structure of ${\mathfrak{A}}$ is isomorphic (as a cylindric algebra
atom structure) to the atom structure ${\cal M}_n$ of all $n$-dimensional basic
matrices over the relation algebra atom structure $\alpha({\bf G})$

nodes.name: isomorphism via $\alpha_m$
nodes.statement: Indeed, for each $m \in {\cal M}_n, \,\ \textrm{let} \,\ \alpha_m = \bigwedge_{i,j<n} \alpha_{ij}. $ Here $ \alpha_{ij}$ is $x_i = x_j$ if $ m_{ij} = 1$' and $R(x_i, x_j)$ otherwise, where $R = m_{ij} \in L$. Then the map $(m \mapsto \alpha^W_m)_{m \in {\cal M}_n}$ is a well - defined isomorphism of $n$-dimensional cylindric algebra atom structures.
nodes.statement_short: Construction: map each basic matrix $m$ to the formula $\alpha_m$ and check it is an isomorphism of atom structures.

nodes.name: Cm$\alpha({\bf G})$ is not representable (chromatic number $N$)
nodes.statement: It can be shown that the complex algebras of this atom structure is not representable, because its chromatic number is finite; indeed it is exactly $N$.
conclusions: the complex algebras of this atom structure is not representable

nodes.statement: Is it possible, thatthe constructed relation algebrais {\it not} in $S{\sf Ra} {\sf CA}_{n+2}$ which is strictly smaller that ${\sf RRA}$.

nodes.statement: But we are also {\it certain } that the complex algebra is not in $S{\sf Ra}{\sf CA}_{n+k}$ for some $k\in \omega$, by the neat embedding theorem for relation algebras, namey, ${\sf RRA}=\bigcap_{k\in \omega}S{\sf Ra}{\sf CA}_{n+k}.$

nodes.statement_short: By the neat embedding theorem ${\sf RRA}=\bigcap_k S{\sf Ra}{\sf CA}_{n+k}$, the complex algebra lies outside some $S{\sf Ra}{\sf CA}_{n+k}$.

nodes.name: clique of a relativized representation
nodes.statement: A clique $C$ of $X$ is a subset of the domain $X$, that can indeed be viewed as a complete graph, in the sense that any two points in it we have $X\models 1(x,y)$, equivalently $(x,y)\in V$, where $V$ is the unit of the relativization.

nodes.name: $n+k$ squareness
nodes.statement: The property of $n+k$ squareness means, then for all cliques $C$ of $X$ with $|C|<n+k$, can always be extended to another clique having at most one more element witnessing composition, so that composition can be preserved in the representation, but only locally.

nodes.statement: For a relation algebra ${\sf R}$ having an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis, let ${\sf Mat}_n{\sf R}$ be the term cylindric algebra of dimension $n$ generated by the basic matrices.

nodes.name: Hodkinson's theorem (atomic RCA$_n$ with non-representable completion)
nodes.statement: Let ${\bf G}$ be a graph that is a disjoint union of cliques having size $n$. Then there is a strongly $n$ homogenious labelled graph $M$, every edge is labelled by an element from ${\bf G}\cup \{\rho\}\times n$, $W\subseteq {}^nM$, such that the set algebra based on $W$ is an atomic ${\mathfrak{A}}\in {\sf RCA}_n$, and there is an atomic ${\sf R}\in {\sf RRA}$ the latter with an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis, such that ${\mathfrak{A}}\cong {\sf Mat}_n{\sf R}$, and the completions of ${\mathfrak{A}}$ and ${\sf R}$ are not representable, hence they are not completely representable.

conclusions: there is a strongly $n$ homogenious labelled graph $M$, every edge is labelled by an element from ${\bf G}\cup \{\rho\}\times n$, $W\subseteq {}^nM$, such that the set algebra based on $W$ is an atomic ${\mathfrak{A}}\in {\sf RCA}_n$
there is an atomic ${\sf R}\in {\sf RRA}$ the latter with an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis, such that ${\mathfrak{A}}\cong {\sf Mat}_n{\sf R}$

nodes.name: evenly distributed triple $e(i,j,k)$
nodes.statement: For $i,j,k\in \omega$ $e(i,j,k)$ abbreviates that $i,j,k$ are {\it evenly distributed}, i.e. $$e(i,j,k)\text { iff } (\exists p,q,r)\{p,q,r\}=\{i,j,k\}, r-q=q-p$$ For example $3,5,7$ are evenly distributed, but $3,5,8$ are not.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: \begin{enumarab} \item Non representabiliy uses the first partition of $H$. Note that $;$ is defined on ${\mathfrak{Cm}}({\cal F})$ so that $$H^P; H^Q=\bigcup \{H^Z: Z\leq P; Q\in {\bold M}\}.$$ So $\bold M$ is isomorphic to a subalgebra of ${\mathfrak{Cm}} F$. But ${\mathfrak{Cm}} F$ can only be represented on infinite sets, while ${\mathfrak{M}}$ only on finite ones, hence we are done. \item The representability of the term algebra uses the second partition. The blow up and blur algebra is ${\cal R}=\{X\subseteq F: X\cap E^W\in Cof(E^W), \forall W\in J\}$. For any $a\in F$ and $W\in J$, let $$U^a=\{X\in R: a\in X\}$$ and $$U^W=\{X\in R: |Z\cap E^W|\geq \omega\}$$ Let $${\sf Uf}=\{U^a: a\in F\}\cup \{U^W: W\in J: |E^W|\geq \omega \}.$$ ${\sf Uf}$ denotes the set of ultrafilters of $\cal R$, that include at least one non-principal ultrafilter, that is an element of the form $U^W$. Let $F,G,K$ be boolean ultrafilters in a relation algebra and let $;$ denote composition. Then $$F;G=\{X;Y: X\in F, Y\in G\}.$$ The triple $(F,G,K)$ is {\it consistent} if the following holds: $$F;G\subseteq K, F;K\subseteq G\text{ and }G;K\subseteq F.$$ So to represent $\cal R$ using $Uf$ as colours, we want to achieve (i) -(iii) below: \begin{enumroman} \item $(U^a,U^b,U^W)$ is consistent whenever $a,b\in H$ and $a;b\in U^W.$ \item $(F,G,K)$ is consistent whenever at least two of $F,G,K$ are non-principal and $F,G,K\in Uf-\{U^{Id}\}.$ \item For any $a,b,c,d\in H$, there is $W\in J'$ such that $a;b\cap c;d\in U^W$. \end{enumroman} Let us see how to represent this algebra. We call $(G,l)$ a {\it consistent coloured graph} if $G$ is a set, $l:G\times G\to Uf$ such that for all $x,y,z\in G$, the following hold: \begin{enumroman} \item $l(x,y)=U^{Id}$ iff $x=y,$ \item $l(x,y)=l(y,x)$ \item The triple $(l(x,y),l(x,z),l(y,z))$ is consistent. \end{enumroman} We say that a consistent coloured graph $(G,l)$ is complete if for all $x,y\in G$, and $F,K\in Uf$, whenever $(l(x,y),F,K)$ is consistent, then there is a node $z$ such that $l(z,x)=F$ and $l(z,y)=K$. We will build a complete consistent graph step-by-step. So assume (inductively) that$(G,l)$ is a consistent coloured graph and $(l(x,y), F, K)$ is a consistent triple. We shall extend $(G,l)$ with a new point $z$ such that $(l(x,y), l(z,x), l(z,y)) =(l(x,y),G,K).$ Let $z\notin G.$ We define $l(z,p)$ for $p\in G$ as follows: $$l(z,x)=F$$ $$l(z,y)=K, \text { and if } p\in G\smallsetminus \{x,y\}, \text { then }$$ $$l(z,p)=U^W\text { for some }W\in J' \text { such that both }$$ $$(U^W, F, l(x,p))\text { and } (U^W, K, l(y,p))\text { are consistent }.$$ Such a $W$ exists by our assumptions (i)-(iii). Conditions (i)-(ii) guarantee that this extension is again a consistent coloured graph. We now show that any non-empty complete coloured graph $(G,l)$ gives a representation for $\cal R.$ For any $X\in R$ define $$rep(X)=\{(u,v)\in G\times G: X\in l(u,v)\}$$ We show that $$rep:{\cal R}\to R(G)$$ is an embedding. $rep$ is a boolean homomorphism because all the labels are ultrafilters. $$rep(Id)=\{(u,u): u\in G\},$$ and for all $X\in R$, $$rep(X)^{-1}=rep(X).$$ The latter follows from the first condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph. From the second condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph, we have: $$rep(X);rep(Y)\subseteq rep(X;Y).$$ Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X), (v,w)\in rep(Y)$ I.e. $X\in l(u,v), Y\in l(v,w).$ Since $(l(u,v), l(v,w), l(u,w))$ is consistent, then $X;Y\in l(u,w)$, i.e. $(u,w)\in rep(X;Y).$ On the other hand, since $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i)-(ii) hold, we have: $$rep(X;Y)\subseteq rep(X);rep(Y),$$ because $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i) and (ii) hold. Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X;Y)$. Then $X;Y\in l(u,v)$. We show that there are $F,K\in {\sf Uf}$ such that $$X\in F, Y\in K \text { and } (l(u,v), F,K)\text { is consistent }.$$ We distinguish between two cases: {\bf Case 1}. $l(u,v)=U^a$ for some $a\in F$. By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$ Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent. {\bf Case 2.} $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$. Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i). Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$ Finally, $rep$ is one to one because $rep(a)\neq \emptyset$ for all $a\in A$. Indeed $(u,v)\in rep(Id)$ for any $u\in G$. Let $a\in H$. Then $(U^{Id}, U^a, U^a)$ is consistent, so there is a $v\in G$ with $l(u,v)=U^a$. Then $(u,v)\in rep(a).$ \end{enumarab}
nodes.statement_short: (1) $\bold M$ embeds in Cm$\cal F$, which has only infinite representations, while $\bold M$ has only finite ones. (2) Build a complete consistent coloured graph step by step with ultrafilters as colours and show $rep$ is an embedding.

nodes.name: atom structures ${\cal F}(l,\mu)$
nodes.statement: Let $l\in \omega$, $l\geq 2$, and let $\mu$ be a non-zero cardinal. Let $I$ be a finite set, $|I|\geq 3l.$ Let $$J=\{(X,n): X\subseteq I, |X|=l,n<\mu\}.$$ Let $H$ be as before, i.e. $$H=\{a_i^{P,W}: i\in \omega, P\in I, W\in J\}.$$ Define $(a_i^{P,S,p}, a_j^{Q,Z,q}, a_k^{R,W,r})$ is consistent ff $S\cap Z\cap W=\emptyset$ or $ e(i,j,k) \text { and } |\{P,Q,R\}|\neq 1.$ Pending on $l$ and $\mu$, let us call these atom structures ${\cal F}(l,\mu).$ Then our first example in is just ${\cal F}(2,1).$ If $\mu\geq \omega$, then $J$ as defined above would be infinite, and ${\sf Uf}$ will be a proper subset of the ultrafilters. It is not difficult to show that if $l\geq \omega$ (and we relax the condition that $I$ be finite), then ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is completely representable, and if $l<\omega$ then ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is not representable. In the former case we have infnitely many colours, so that the chromatic nmber of the graph is infinite, while in the second case the chromatic number is infinite. Informally, if the blurs get arbitarily large, then in the limit, the resulting algebra will be completely representable, and so its complex algebra will be representable. If we take, a sequence of blurs, each finite, but increasing in size we get a sequence of algebras that are not completely representable, and the sequence of their complex algebras will not be representable. The limit of the former, will be completely representable (with an infinite set of blurs); its completion will be the limit of the second sequence of non representable, will be representable. Either construction can be used to achieve this. This phenomena has many reincarnations in the literature. One is the following: It is is nothing more than Monk's classical non finite axiomatizability result; it gives a sequence of non representable algebras whose ultraproduct is completely representable.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.3
nodes.statement: {Proof} For the second we use the second construction. Let ${\cal D}$ be a non- trivial ultraproduct of the atom structures ${\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$. Then ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\cal D}$ is completely representable. Thus ${\mathfrak{Tm}}{\cal F}(i,1)$ are ${\sf RRA}$'s without a complete representation while their ultraproduct has a complete representation. Also ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$ are non representable with a completely representable ultraproduct. This yields the desired result. We prove the cylindric case. Take ${\bf G}_i$ to be the disjoint union of cliques of size $n(n-1)/2+i$. Let $\alpha_i$ be the corresponding atom astructure of ${\mathfrak{A}}_i$, as constructed above. Then ${\mathfrak{Cm}} {\mathfrak{A}}_i$ is not representable, but $\prod_{i\in \omega}{\mathfrak{Cm}}{\mathfrak{A}}_i={\mathfrak{Cm}}(\prod_{i\in \omega}{\mathfrak{A}}_i)$. Then the latter is based on the disjoint union of the cliques which is arbitrarily large, hence is representable.

This is the definition. But it is not hard to show that this is equivalent to the simpler condition that for all cliques $C$ of $X$ with $|C|<n+k$, all $x,y\in C$ and $a,b\in {\mathfrak{Cm}}\alpha({\bf G})$, $X\models (a;b)(x,y)$ there exists $z\in X$ such that $C\cup \{z\}$ is a clique and $X\models a(x,z)\land b(z,y)$.

nodes.name: Represent the term algebra via a complete consistent coloured graph
nodes.statement: The representability of the term algebra uses the second partition. The blow up and blur algebra is ${\cal R}=\{X\subseteq F: X\cap E^W\in Cof(E^W), \forall W\in J\}$. For any $a\in F$ and $W\in J$, let $$U^a=\{X\in R: a\in X\}$$ and $$U^W=\{X\in R: |Z\cap E^W|\geq \omega\}$$ Let $${\sf Uf}=\{U^a: a\in F\}\cup \{U^W: W\in J: |E^W|\geq \omega \}.$$ ${\sf Uf}$ denotes the set of ultrafilters of $\cal R$, that include at least one non-principal ultrafilter, that is an element of the form $U^W$. Let $F,G,K$ be boolean ultrafilters in a relation algebra and let $;$ denote composition. Then $$F;G=\{X;Y: X\in F, Y\in G\}.$$ The triple $(F,G,K)$ is {\it consistent} if the following holds: $$F;G\subseteq K, F;K\subseteq G\text{ and }G;K\subseteq F.$$ So to represent $\cal R$ using $Uf$ as colours, we want to achieve (i) -(iii) below: \begin{enumroman} \item $(U^a,U^b,U^W)$ is consistent whenever $a,b\in H$ and $a;b\in U^W.$ \item $(F,G,K)$ is consistent whenever at least two of $F,G,K$ are non-principal and $F,G,K\in Uf-\{U^{Id}\}.$ \item For any $a,b,c,d\in H$, there is $W\in J'$ such that $a;b\cap c;d\in U^W$. \end{enumroman} Let us see how to represent this algebra. We show that there are $F,K\in {\sf Uf}$ such that $$X\in F, Y\in K \text { and } (l(u,v), F,K)\text { is consistent }.$$ We distinguish between two cases: {\bf Case 1}. $l(u,v)=U^a$ for some $a\in F$. By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$ Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent. {\bf Case 2.} $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$. Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i). Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$ Finally, $rep$ is one to one because $rep(a)\neq \emptyset$ for all $a\in A$. Indeed $(u,v)\in rep(Id)$ for any $u\in G$.
